  • Decreased internal ticket volumes by nearly 8 percent (source: LoanPro). Lenders on the platform report fewer support escalations as agents resolve more cases during the initial call.
  • Account summaries in under 15 seconds (source: LoanPro internal benchmarks). The narrative summary transforms raw borrower data into a coherent account story within 15 seconds of opening an account, replacing what previously took agents 3–5 minutes of manual navigation.
  • Consistent servicing quality. The assistant provides the same level of account context and action recommendations to agents across the platform, reducing variability tied to individual experience levels.
  • Compliance-aligned interaction logging. Every action and query the agent makes through the AI assistant is logged, providing an auditable record of interactions during borrower conversations.
  • Responsible AI controls. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content filtering and grounding validation to agent responses alongside LoanPro’s compliance guardrails and role-based access controls (RBAC), keeping outputs within policy before they reach a servicing agent and the borrower.
“The AI assistant has changed how servicing agents work. Instead of spending the first few minutes of every call navigating screens and assembling context, agents now open an account and immediately see the full picture with prescriptive recommendations around the next actions to take. That time savings compounds across thousands of calls.”
— Colin Terry, Chief Product Officer, LoanPro

Looking ahead

Building on the success of the servicing agent assistant, LoanPro and AllCloud are expanding their collaboration. The teams are developing additional AI agents to extend intelligent capabilities across more parts of the lending workflow, moving beyond servicing into areas such as collections and origination support.

The modular, multi-agent architecture makes this expansion practical. New agents can be built and deployed independently using the same Amazon Bedrock AgentCore infrastructure, without redesigning the core system. As the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore continue to evolve, LoanPro plans to incorporate new capabilities as they become available.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how LoanPro, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, and AllCloud built a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help servicing agents resolve borrower calls faster and more consistently. The solution retrieves data autonomously, generates account summaries in real time, and recommends next-best actions, reducing customer call times by up to 15 percent.

If you are building agentic AI solutions for customer-facing workflows, here are some resources to explore:

  • Amazon Bedrock: Fully managed service for building with foundation models.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Infrastructure to deploy, manage, and scale AI agents.
  • Strands Agents SDK: Open source framework for building AI agents with tool use.
  • AWS Generative AI Innovation Center: Accelerate your generative AI journey with AWS experts.

To get started, explore the Strands Agents SDK on GitHub for building multi-agent systems, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation for deploying agents at scale, or visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center to learn how AWS experts can help accelerate your own AI initiative.

About the authors

item.title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform…
item.description: Full title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams

Companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use. The nondeterministic nature of generative AI models introduces a complexity that previous software development practices didn’t anticipate. Consider a real estate app that generates property listings from retrieved data: does it accurately reflect the property, or hallucinate features that don’t exist? Or a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases: can you verify that it doesn’t surface confidential information?

Until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference. Models didn’t reason, use tools, or take actions. When the conversation extended to model-powered systems, it covered statistically bounded situations you could test against known inputs. Generative AI powered applications and agents changed this. The systems now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, expanding both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover.

Organizations are turning Responsible AI, which includes the pillars of security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance into a growth strategy by addressing its expanding scope early. When enterprises adopt agentic AI at scale, the positive and negative impacts come hand in hand. As Wade and Wirtz observe in the Harvard Business Review, trust is becoming a competitive differentiator. The same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate, and organizations that govern them earn stakeholder confidence. Robinhood, for example, built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance. They achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. Structuring these practices across platform maturity is the next step. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Application teams. Application teams, sometimes called Workstream teams, build and own agents on the platform.

This post provides a condensed, actionable roadmap for the Platform team and Application teams building on agentic AI. It’s designed to be read together: the Platform team sets up the guardrails. Application teams build within them. Both need a shared language for where they are and what good looks like. We provide a Responsible AI Assessment Skill, that maps the AWS Responsible AI Lens pillars to a three-phase maturity model: governance foundations, pilot deployment, and evaluation and hardening. For each phase, it shows which responsible AI pillars are critical and when to revisit them. An accompanying scorecard lets both application teams and the platform team assess where they are today and iterate as their applications mature.

Note: This post covers the key questions to ask at each phase. It leaves out step-by-step implementation details. This post also doesn’t provide legal or compliance advice. Always consult your legal team.

The challenge

In conversations with customers building agentic AI platforms, four challenges surface consistently.

  • Unpredictable runtime behavior: nondeterministic outputs, goal drift, and cascading failures where one agent error propagates across services. A financial services company in Germany found that multi-agent orchestration amplified a single misclassification into policy violations across three downstream services.
  • Data exposure and authority boundaries: Scope every agent to its intended tenants, data, systems, and actions. Isolate session context so each session starts with data residency at the access layer, and grant privileged access through least-privilege, task-bound permissions that agents can’t modify themselves. Agents then act only in the systems and with the authority they were explicitly given.
  • Regulatory velocity: EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, and upcoming legislation are creating compliance requirements faster than governance can adapt. Proving compliance for nondeterministic systems requires continuous evaluation, which should be monitored and revisited with a predefined cadence (for example, daily, weekly, or monthly).
  • Team collaboration: organizations lack a shared framework defining who owns what across the agent lifecycle. A media company in the UK flagged that segregation of duty between developer and deployment teams is undefined for agent workloads. The Platform team builds guardrails that application teams work around, and application teams defer responsibility they assume the platform handles.

Figure 1: Agentic AI platforms introduce novel challenges regarding responsible AI.

Solution: A three-phase responsible AI maturity framework

In this post, we define an agentic AI platform as described in AgentOps: Operationalize agentic AI at scale with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a system for building, deploying, and operating AI agents securely at scale, covering governance, build and operations, evaluation, and observability. Your responsible AI posture should mature progressively alongside this platform. We break the journey into three phases and present prioritized responsible AI pillars across a customizable 12-week implementation timeline, allowing the platform team to establish a solid responsible AI foundation while their first use cases take shape.

Figure 2: Overview of the proposed responsible AI maturity framework for agentic AI platforms. Teams integrate responsible AI over three phases.

Phase 1: Governance foundation

Focus pillars: Governance, security and privacy

In this phase, assess project fit, risks, and ethics, secure legal and compliance approvals, and define the trust model for AI agents. The application teams classify risks for each planned use case using a risk rubric. The Platform team focuses on establishing the core landing zone infrastructure, for example, setting up the overarching monitoring and access control, and governing newly onboarded agents and use cases from the start.

Critical tasks to consider in this phase include:

Security and privacy

  • Evaluate access to data and systems needed by each agent and assess potential impact. This lays the foundation for the knowledge grounding strategy.
  • Implement foundational data security and data exfiltration protection with data classification, data access control, logging, data integrity, and data access monitoring.
  • Build a map of the data that is shared between agents like organizational knowledge bases and the subjective data like context graphs which individual agents might need. Then establish access boundaries and assign read/write permissions accordingly.

Governance

  • Define a risk classification rubric aligned to your regulatory obligations (EU AI Act risk tiers, financial services industry requirements, and so on). Assign Low / Medium / High / Unacceptable risk levels to each planned use case and document the control requirements each risk level triggers. Gather relevant documentation and traceability requirements.
  • Before onboarding agents, the underlying models need to go through a vetting procedure. The procedure covers a series of evaluations with safety and reliability criteria. Catalog approved models based on capability, latency, and cost.
  • Implement a process to centrally register and govern products like agents, shared tools and skills deployed in your organization for centralized visibility and consumption. Every product gets registered with owner, risk tier, and regulatory scope. If a resource (agent, tool, skill) isn’t in the registry, it can’t be discovered and managed by the organization.

Phase 2: Pilot deployment

Focus pillars: Safety, veracity and robustness, controllability, security and privacy

Deploy your first agent that serves measurable business value. With the template and developer guidance provided from the Platform team, application teams implement orchestration patterns, memory, guardrail baselines, knowledge grounding, and tool use patterns. Risks identified in the foundation phase must now be addressed through a set of concrete controls in a pilot implementation.

In this phase, application teams consider the following concerns:

Safety

  • Guardrails. Platform team establishes foundational personally identifiable information (PII) redaction filters for model I/O and tool calls. Provide a set of guardrails rules ready to be applied. Application teams then set content moderation thresholds explicitly based on the use case the agent serves. Configure human escalation for low-confidence responses.
  • Policies. Define which agent can access what tool and how. Augment with fallback scenarios in case of policy violations.

Veracity and robustness

  • Knowledge grounding with checks: Even with the right context, models can still hallucinate or misrepresent the provided sources. Therefore, configure contextual grounding checks to verify every response is correctly grounded in relevant data. For regulated use cases, activate automated reasoning for verifiable outputs. Implement a process to curate and update your knowledge sources. Define how out-of-domain requests are classified and handled.

Controllability

  • Implement a process for Human-in-the-loop approval for high-risk or on-behalf-of actions as circuit breakers. Define criteria for when an agent must defer to a human approver/reviewer (for example, confidence below threshold, safety guardrail triggered, or a high-stakes decision). Log escalation events for later audit and analysis.
  • Provide permission audits to the end-user to grant/revoke access provided by human users or agents that granted permissions to sub-agents to gain transparent control.
  • Activate end-to-end observability with session-level, trace-level, and span-level telemetry. Emit structured traces for agent decisions, guardrail invocations, and tool calls. Implement distributed tracing across multi-agent and multi-tool workflows to support full reconstruction of agent reasoning paths. Add dashboards for 360-degree observability and cost-control.

Security and privacy

  • Establish least-privilege access controls. Define policy-based authorization rules for tool-level access using declarative policy languages. Apply granular access policies for agent actions and per knowledge source.

Phase 3: Evaluation and hardening

Focus pillars: Fairness, explainability, transparency, security and privacy

You have seen your first agent deliver business value. But how can you demonstrate it to a regulator, an auditor, or a board? How do you detect and help prevent unauthorized events on the system? In the third phase, evaluation stress-tests the fairness thresholds, and bias benchmarking. Hardening turns those findings into fixes.

This phase includes the following workstreams:

Fairness

  • Model-level fairness testing: Check model cards for fairness metrics and restrict model access to a list of pre-approved models tested for common biases. In case there is no metric provided, test bias and alignment yourself using established benchmark sets such as Compositional Evaluation Benchmark (CEB) or Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM). Monitor whether outputs and routing treat demographic groups equitably.
  • Agent-level fairness testing: Evaluate whether end-to-end agent routing, including tool selection, and resource allocation treats user groups equitably.
  • Fairness regression monitoring: Set up automated pipelines to detect fairness drift over time as models are updated or new data sources are added.

Transparency

  • Enforceable transparency for machine generated content: Attach machine-readable provenance labels to every reusable output, so downstream consumers can verify origin. Enforce mandatory AI-presence disclosure in user-facing interactions.
  • Decision audit trails: Each agent action is logged with enough detail to reconstruct the reasoning path for a given outcome. For instance, what did the agent access, when and with which identity.

Explainability

  • Compile an audit report for a fictional audit or appeal: Make sure you can quickly assemble the relevant data and understand how a decision was made.
  • User-facing explanations: Provide end-users with on-demand, plain-language summaries of why an agent took a specific action or made a recommendation.

Security and privacy

  • Continuous evaluation: Set up evaluation pipelines and evaluate before and after deployment. Document the results. Implement alerting mechanisms to be notified when metrics fall below a predefined quality threshold.
  • Conduct penetration testing and red-team evaluations targeting agent-specific threat models: prompt injection, tenant isolation under concurrent access, token exchange with misconfigured profiles, and long-running async agent tasks. Define a Security Incident Response runbook specific to AI agent safety events. Configure automated alerting for safety-critical events.
  • Fine-tune release criteria (evaluation scores, security scan results, fairness metrics) iteratively based on production feedback. Build deployment gates into your continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline. Nothing reaches production without meeting the release criteria for its risk tier.

When to revisit

Responsible AI isn’t a one-time implementation. As the platform evolves, each dimension must be periodically reassessed. The following table gives some examples to define both standing review cadences and event-driven triggers for re-evaluation.

Standing Cadence
Compliance assessment for in-scope agents: Documentation refresh, re-run evidence collection, human oversight logs. Review risk classification, incident post-mortems. Review onboarding and decommissioning procedures. Continuous evaluation with drift detection autonomy, risk scoring and alerting. Track false positive and false negative rates of Guardrails and adjust when needed. Refresh knowledge bases continuously, remove outdated documents.
Triggers
New use case is onboarded. New model added or model updates. New tools added. Onboarding new customer segment. New risk identified, for example, a new security threat discovered. Agent updated, for example, a new system prompt. Compliance or regulatory change. Agent behaviors change.

Example use case and implementation

Consider the following case: A bank builds a multi-agent loan processing platform. The platform features an intake agent, risk scoring agent, compliance agent, and customer communication agent.

Phase 1 (Governance foundation): The platform team gathers legal requirements for their use case, for example those stemming from the EU AI Act and financial regulation, and registers agents at High-risk tier (financial decisions affecting individuals) using the AWS Agent Registry. They use a secure landing zone built with AWS Control Tower with foundational logging and access control active and configure tenant isolation to help prevent cross-customer leakage. The team documents residual risk and scope for each agent: for example, if the intake agent produces unexpected data, the risk scoring agent processes its output without independent verification.

Phase 2 (Pilot deployment: Validation and rollout): Risk scoring uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases grounded in regulatory lending documentation. Automated Reasoning checks verify denial decisions conform to documented criteria (conformance, not causal explanation). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redact PII data before customer communication. To address the multi-agent trust gap: the scoring agent confirms key applicant data from source systems rather than solely relying on the intake agent’s extraction. Each agent is bounded to required tools through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and the team uses Policies in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to further restrict the risk scoring agent to read-only access on the customer segment the agent is approved for. A case where the Automated Reasoning check returns a result other than VALID (for example, SATISFIABLE or TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS), or where the applicant’s risk score falls within the marginal band (for example, ±5 points of the threshold), is automatically escalated to a human credit specialist (human-in-the-loop review) before the decision is communicated. Escalation events are logged with the triggering condition for audit.

Phase 3 (Evaluation and hardening: Continuous monitoring): Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, run on every pipeline push. CI/CD blocks deployment if an evaluation result is below releasing criterion or per-subgroup fairness metrics drifts beyond threshold. Red-team exercises (independent security team) test realistic security threats on the intake agent to verify that it can’t influence scoring. Human review of denial decisions, moving to after-the-fact review through an appeals process after 2,000 aligned decisions over 60 days. AI usage in the decision process is disclosed transparently to customers. Every automated decision is traced end-to-end using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It captures OpenTelemetry spans that can be automatically aggregated into a single distributed trace ready for auditing and appeals.

How to measure maturity

Frameworks serve as aspirations, while measurements provide accountability. Questions like “Can you list the risk tier for a use case?” will necessarily arise when the platform is operational from stakeholders like CISOs or auditors. To leave you prepared, we provide a repository with a set of questions that you can use to gauge your current posture and identify improvement areas before your system goes live.

We also package the questionnaire as a portable skill for AI Agents like Amazon Quick, and AI coding assistants like Kiro, Claude Code, and Codex. The AI walks you through each phase and assesses your responsible AI posture along the dimensions on a scale from 1–5. Scores below 4 indicate substantial risks that should be remediated. Scores of 4 or higher indicate residual risk that might be acceptable when acknowledged on a case-by-case basis. The AI also provides actionable recommendations for improving your Responsible AI posture.

Figure 3: A portable AI skill that helps teams assess their Responsible AI posture through a set of questions.

Conclusion

Responsible AI (RAI) is a continuous, evolving effort. We recommend organizations implement RAI pillars through the AgentOps journey. These best practices cover governance policies, evaluation gates, and production telemetry into agentic AI platforms. This creates the feedback loop that keeps fairness, safety, and transparency continuously measured and improved.

This framework is a starting point, not an exhaustive compliance checklist. RAI practices vary by industry, use case, and requirements. Organizations should consult their own legal, compliance, and ethics teams to tailor these recommendations to their specific regulatory obligations and risk profiles.

For a comprehensive treatment of responsible AI across workload types, refer to the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens, which provides detailed best practices, design principles, and evaluation criteria for each of the eight pillars discussed in this post. For industry-specific guidance, consult the Financial Services Industry Lens and the Healthcare Industry Lens, which address sector-specific regulatory and ethical requirements. Get started today by installing the RAI assessment skill from this repository and evaluating your organization’s RAI posture with your preferred AI agent.

About the authors

item.title: How ArisGlobal scaled generative AI inference on Amazon Bedr…
item.description: Full title: How ArisGlobal scaled generative AI inference on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How ArisGlobal scaled generative AI inference on Amazon Bedrock

ArisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology spanning pharmacovigilance, regulatory, medical affairs, clinical, and quality functions, developed NavaX, an AI engine purpose-built for life sciences on Amazon Bedrock, to automate adverse-event case processing. ArisGlobal chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, EU geographic cross-Region inference, and managed prompt caching. As enterprise customers added distinct compliance requirements, the shared prompt prefix grew by about 150% over 6 months, while per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%.

ArisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request. That left the growing shared prompt prefix outside the cache. By reversing the order and caching the shared prefix instead, ArisGlobal reduced effective input cost and supported additional tenants without proportional cost growth.

Who is ArisGlobal?

ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information. LifeSphere serves pharmaceutical companies globally, including multiple Top 20 pharma organizations by revenue (source: ArisGlobal press release). The entire system runs on AWS.

LifeSphere NavaX is ArisGlobal’s AI engine that transforms drug safety from a system of record into a system of strategic advantage. ArisGlobal productionized their first generative AI solution on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic’s Claude in March 2025. According to ArisGlobal’s internal production telemetry, they have processed over 1 million real transactions in regulated pharmaceutical environments, handling billions of tokens across multiple enterprise tenants. Model availability varies by Region. See Model support by AWS Region.

How NavaX processes an adverse event case

When a pharmaceutical company receives an adverse-event report, typically a multipage PDF describing a patient’s reaction to a medication, NavaX’s Dynamic Data Extraction (DDE) agent extracts around 130 fields. These fields include patient demographics, suspect drugs, reporter information, event timelines, seriousness criteria, and regulatory classifications. Because this content includes protected health information, ArisGlobal applies responsible-AI controls as a standard part of its production deployment. It draws on capabilities such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter content and detect or mask sensitive information. Extracted fields are also validated against the schema and grounded in the source document.

This extraction happens across multiple sequential requests to the model. Each request focuses on a different section of the case form, and each carries:

  • System instructions — model behavior rules, output format specifications, and regulatory compliance constraints.
  • Customer-specific rules — per-tenant extraction logic, field mappings, and business rules that differ by pharmaceutical company.
  • Extraction schema — around 130 target fields with types, validation rules, and few-shot examples.
  • The source document — the adverse event PDF (often 10–200 pages).

Two inputs repeat at different scopes. The shared prompt prefix includes the system rules, extraction schema, and few-shot examples. It repeats across requests, cases, and tenants using the same agent. The source document repeats only for the requests associated with one case.

The prompt bloat problem

When NavaX launched with its first enterprise tenant, the system prompt was lean. As ArisGlobal onboarded additional pharmaceutical companies, each brought specific requirements:

  • Custom field mappings (Tenant A maps reaction onset differently from Tenant B).
  • Regulatory jurisdiction rules (EU ICSR compared with FDA MedWatch and PMDA formatting).
  • Company-specific business logic for seriousness assessment and causality.
  • Per-tenant few-shot examples calibrated to each company’s historical cases.

Over 6 months, the shared prompt prefix grew from approximately 72,000 to 180,000 tokens, a 150% increase. With multiple sequential requests per case, per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%.

The prefix grew with every tenant and was reprocessed on every request, so prompt growth compounded with transaction volume.

Table 1 compares the original document-first request order with the production prompt-first design.

AspectFirst approachProduction design
Request orderPer-case document, cache checkpoint, shared prompt prefixShared prompt prefix, cache checkpoint, per-case document
Cached prefixThe document, which changes for every caseThe shared prompt prefix, which repeats across requests
Reuse scopeOnly the remaining requests for one caseRequests across cases and tenants using the same agent
Cost effectThe growing prompt is repeatedly processed at the full input rateFleet-wide prompt reuse supports sublinear cost growth
EU routingEU geographic cross-Region inference remains unchangedEU geographic cross-Region inference remains unchanged

Amazon Bedrock prompt caching strategies

Amazon Bedrock prompt caching reduces latency and input token costs by caching a contiguous prompt prefix from the start of a request through a cache checkpoint. A later request with the same prefix can read cached tokens at a reduced rate instead of processing them again. Cache entries have a time-to-live (TTL) that resets after a successful cache hit.

Caching is prefix-based rather than block-based. Request sections are evaluated in sequence—tools, system, then messages—so changing an earlier section invalidates matching content that follows it.

Cache checkpoints (explicit control)

With explicit cache checkpoints, you can choose the exact prefix boundary. Supported Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request.

  • Place each checkpoint after a stable, reusable prefix.
  • Meet the model-specific minimum prefix size. For Claude Sonnet 4.5 the minimum is 1,024 tokens (see supported models and Regions).
  • Checkpoints are evaluated in this order: tools, system, and messages.
  • Changing an earlier section invalidates cache matches for later sections.
  • The default TTL is 5 minutes. Select models support a 1-hour TTL by setting "ttl": "1h". Longer-TTL entries must precede shorter-TTL entries.

Simplified cache management (automated)

With simplified cache management, you place one checkpoint after static content. Amazon Bedrock searches backward from that point for the longest matching prefix, up to about 20 content blocks.

  • One checkpoint can locate the longest matching prefix automatically.
  • Use explicit checkpoints when stable content extends beyond the lookback range.

What ArisGlobal cached, and what they deliberately did not

ArisGlobal uses one explicit checkpoint immediately after the shared prompt prefix, which is sent first. The per-case document follows the checkpoint and is processed on each request.

This reverses the initial request order. Because only a prefix can be cached, ordering determines which content can be reused.

The launch design: Prioritizing document reuse

The first design put the 10–200 page source document at the start of each request and placed the checkpoint after it. The shared prompt prefix and section-specific question followed the checkpoint.

{
  "modelId": "anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        {
          "text": "[Full adverse event PDF content]..." // <-- Document sent FIRST
        },
        {
          "cachePoint": {"type": "default"} // <-- Checkpoint right after the document
        },
        {
          "text": "[System instructions + compliance rules + schema +
          few-shot examples + customer-specific prompt]..."
          // <-- After the checkpoint: never cached
        },
        {
          "text": "Extract fields for Section 3: Suspect Drug Information"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The design reused the document within one case: the first request wrote it to cache, and later requests for that case read it at the reduced rate.

The next case used a different document and required a new cache write, so reuse never extended across cases or tenants.

More importantly, the shared prompt prefix remained after the checkpoint and was processed at the full input rate on every request. The content driving the cost curve was excluded from the cache.

The evolved production design: Prioritizing shared-prefix reuse

The production design changed the order rather than adding another checkpoint: the shared prompt prefix comes first, the checkpoint follows it, and the document comes last.

The same checkpoint now creates a reusable fleet-wide cache entry:

  • Before — the cached document prefix was unique to one case and the shared prompt was never cached.
  • After — the cached shared prompt prefix repeats across requests, cases, and tenants using the same agent.

ArisGlobal gave up limited document reuse within one case and gained prompt reuse across the fleet. The shared prefix is also the part that grows as customers are added.

Updated implementation

{
  "modelId": "anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",
  "system": [
    {
      "text": "[Shared system instructions + compliance rules +
      base extraction schema + few-shot examples]..."
    },
    {
      "cachePoint": {"type": "default"} // <-- Checkpoint after the stable prompt
    }
  ],
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": [
        {
          "text": "[Full adverse event PDF content — sits after the
          checkpoint, not cached]..."
        },
        {
          "text": "Extract fields for Section 5: Event Assessment"
          // <-- Only this changes per request
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

For most active accounts, cases arrive about every 5 minutes per tenant and multiple tenants run concurrently. This traffic keeps the shared prefix warm during business hours because each cache hit resets the TTL.

Caching both the prompt and the document

A second checkpoint after the document would cache a combined prefix consisting of the shared prompt and that case’s document. The entry would still be unique to one case.

ArisGlobal therefore prioritized the prefix whose reads amortize across the fleet. The shared prompt prefix scales across cases and tenants. The per-case document does not.

In production, 65% of input tokens on a typical request are served from the shared prompt cache. Figure 1 shows cache reads consistently exceeding cache writes.

Figure 1: Amazon CloudWatch prompt-cache usage. The blue cache-read series rises to roughly 10 times the cache-write series during periods of production traffic

Results

Caching the shared prompt prefix produced the following results while the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile remained in place:

  • 65% of input tokens served from cache at the reduced read rate.
  • Up to 25% lower end-to-end latency on cached production requests.
  • Approximately 50% lower effective input cost.
  • Approximately 40% lower overall monthly inference spend at more than 19 billion tokens per month.
  • Around 15% more enterprise tenants onboarded without proportional cost increases.
  • EU geographic routing unchanged. Prompt caching operates within the existing inference configuration.

Figure 2: End-to-end invocation latency. The chart shows a lower and more stable latency range after prompt-cache adoption

Figure 3: Invocation count. The chart shows sustained production request volume while inference spend grew less than proportionally

Based on ArisGlobal’s production billing data, serving 65% of input tokens from cache reduced effective input cost by approximately 50%. At more than 19 billion tokens per month, this produced approximately 40% overall monthly savings in inference spend.

Note: All performance and cost figures in this section reflect ArisGlobal’s production metrics as reported to AWS. Results will vary based on prompt structure, traffic patterns, and cache hit rates.

Production learnings

ArisGlobal’s experience offers guidance for many workloads with large, repeated prompt prefixes:

Cache what repeats, not what is largest. A large per-case document offers limited reuse, while a byte-identical shared prompt prefix can serve requests across the fleet.

Put stable content first. Order tool definitions, system instructions, schemas, and examples before the checkpoint. Place tenant identifiers, case data, and the per-request question afterward.

Use fleet traffic to amortize cache writes. Requests from tenants using the same agent can read the same prefix, and cache hits reset the TTL. For sporadic traffic, evaluate the 1-hour TTL on supported models.

Reduce avoidable calls. Each call still processes the uncached document, so bundle sequential questions when output limits and schema requirements permit.

Keep the prefix byte-identical. Timestamps, request IDs, tenant names, and reordered tool definitions can cause misses. Move every dynamic element after the checkpoint.

Monitor the production baseline. Track cache reads, cache writes, and total input tokens in CloudWatch. Alert on a sustained drop below the normal 65% cache-hit baseline rather than using an incompatible 80% threshold.

Check model-specific limits. Prefix minimums and TTL options vary by model. Claude Sonnet 4.5 requires at least 1,024 tokens for a cache checkpoint.

Conclusion

ArisGlobal combined EU geographic cross-Region inference with prompt caching aimed at the right content. Caching the stable shared prefix instead of the per-case document reduced effective input cost by approximately 50%, contributed to approximately 40% overall monthly inference savings, and supported around 15% more enterprise tenants without proportional cost increases.

The key lesson is that cache value depends on reuse, not size. For multi-tenant agentic workloads, a repeated shared prompt prefix can be more valuable than a larger document that changes for every case.

To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock prompt caching documentation, the cross-Region inference guide, and the AWS blog post Effectively use prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock.

About the authors

item.title: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon…
item.description: Full title: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

Users of a knowledge-grounded application expect it to remember them, not only to search well. They ask follow-up questions that make sense only in the context of the previous turn. They expect an answer about a policy or a procedure to reflect what they told the application about themselves last month. And they still expect every answer to be grounded in the documents they are allowed to read, with citations. Whether the application is a customer support assistant, a document chat inside a SaaS product, or an internal assistant over company policies, the expectation is the same.

Meeting that expectation is hard, because the context that would sharpen a search lives outside the knowledge base. A user’s location, role, or product tier was often mentioned in an unrelated conversation weeks ago. To use it, the application has to store every conversation, extract durable facts from it, decide which facts matter for the current question, and inject them into the request. When many users share the application, every one of those steps also has to be isolated per user, and so does every document.

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now take over these steps: storing each conversation, extracting facts from it, and bringing the relevant facts into the search. You turn this on by adding a memoryConfiguration to the AgenticRetrieveStream request, which makes AgentCore memory a retrieval source alongside your knowledge base. Within the same call, the service restores the conversation, and the planner decides on its own when a fact about the user would help. It retrieves that fact from long-term memory and uses it to compose the sub-queries it sends to the knowledge base. After generating the answer, the service saves the turn back to memory. The same request carries a userContext, so the knowledge base returns only the documents that the user’s access control lists (ACLs) allow. The integration is opt-in and backward compatible. Your application keeps only what is genuinely yours: authenticating the user and passing who they are.

This post shows how to build such an assistant for many users who share one knowledge base and one memory resource. Each user sees only the documents they may read, and each user’s memory stays private. The running example is an internal employee assistant for AnyCompany, a fictional company. Employees sign in with Amazon Cognito and ask questions over HR policies, IT guides, engineering runbooks, and sales plans. We show how to read the user’s identity from the Cognito ID token, how to pass it to AgenticRetrieveStream for document ACLs and for memory, how to design memory namespaces for many users, and how to read the trace to see when the planner used memory. Finally, we make AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforce per-user memory isolation even when application code gets it wrong. If you deployed the application from Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, this post replaces its “persist conversation history yourself” step.

Solution overview

AnyCompany keeps its documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). One managed knowledge base syncs them through an ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data source. A global ACL file in the same bucket says which employees may read each folder: everyone reads HR and IT, only engineers read the engineering runbooks, and only salespeople read the commission plan. One AgentCore memory resource is shared by every employee. Amazon Cognito authenticates employees, and its ID token supplies two claims: the sub (user ID) identifies the user’s memory, and the verified email identifies the user to the knowledge base’s ACL filter. Three test users sign in: two engineers, Maya and Liam, and one salesperson, Sofia. The trace excerpts in this post are taken from a run of the sample application in the GitHub repository.

Figure 1: Architecture of the memory-aware employee assistant. The application authenticates the user and constructs the request (steps 1–4). Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base restores the session, retrieves information, returns an answer, and saves the exchange to AgentCore memory (steps 5–8). Short-term events and long-term records belong to the same memory resource.

  • The employee signs in with Cognito and receives an ID token, a JSON Web Token (JWT) signed by the user pool.
  • The application’s API validates the token — an Amazon API Gateway JWT authorizer in production, a small FastAPI service in the sample. Unauthenticated requests do not reach the handler.
  • The handler reads two claims from the verified token: sub becomes the memory actorId and namespace, and email becomes the userContext.userId. The client body carries only { question, sessionId? }. The handler then assumes the application’s IAM role for this user, with the session tag userId=<sub>.
  • The handler calls AgenticRetrieveStream with the knowledge base as the retriever, userContext, and a memoryConfiguration bound to this user.
  • Managed Knowledge Base restores the conversation history from short-term memory (STM) in AgentCore memory for the actor and session identified by sessionBinding.
  • Managed Knowledge Base retrieves from the knowledge base with ACL filtering based on userContext. It can also retrieve the user’s configured long-term memory through speculative retrieval or memory searches selected by the planner.
  • Managed Knowledge Base streams a cited answer and trace events back to the handler. The handler records the traces with a correlation ID and forwards the answer and trace information to the UI.
  • With persistenceMode: DEFAULT, the service saves the question and generated answer to the session. AgentCore memory then extracts long-term records asynchronously according to the configured strategies.

Figure 2: One AgenticRetrieveStream turn with userContext and memoryConfiguration. Everything between the first and last arrow is the service’s work.

Managed Knowledge Base owns ingestion, ACL filtering, indexing, ranking, planning, retrieval, and generation. With memoryConfiguration, it also owns session restore, memory search, and persistence. AgentCore memory owns storage, retention, encryption, and extraction. Your application owns authentication, the UI, and reading the user’s identity from the token. There is no conversation table: when the UI lists or reopens a conversation, it reads the same memory resource.

How identity maps to the request

Every value is derived by the application from the verified ID token. None comes from the request body.

Request fieldDerived fromWhat it scopesEnforced by
userContext.userIdID token email (verified, immutable in the pool)Which documents can be retrievedKnowledge base ACL filtering
memoryConfiguration.sessionBinding.actorIdID token subWhose short-term memory is restored and written, and the {actorId} in long-term namespacesAgentCore memory keying, plus an IAM condition
memoryConfiguration.sessionBinding.sessionIdGenerated by the application for a new conversation. Listed with ListSessionsWhich conversation within that actorKeyed under the actorId
memoryConfiguration.retrievalConfigs[0].namespacePath/anycompany/<sub>Which long-term records the planner may searchIAM condition

Two different claims do two different jobs. The knowledge base identifies users by email, because that is what the connected data source records in its ACLs. Memory needs an actorId that never changes and is never reused. The Cognito sub is both. An email address can be changed, or reassigned to a new employee after someone leaves, and that person would then inherit the old memory. You can use another stable user ID from your own user store as the actorId. What matters is that it never moves to a different person.

Prerequisites

  • This walkthrough uses a managed knowledge base and an AgentCore memory resource in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2). As described in the agentic retrieval documentation, the memory resource used with this integration must be in the same AWS account as the knowledge base and in the ACTIVE state.
  • Python 3.10 or later and Boto3 1.43.72 or later.
  • Permission to create an S3 bucket, a Cognito user pool, IAM roles, a knowledge base, and a memory resource. The sample’s infra/setup.py creates all of these resources idempotently.

Solution walkthrough

The following steps create the knowledge base and its data source, set up the memory resource and Amazon Cognito, build the request, and read the trace to confirm the result.

Step 1: Create the knowledge base with an ACL-enabled data source

A managed knowledge base needs no vector store:

Configure the service role for your setup by following Create a service role for managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and pass its ARN in roleArn. For model access requirements, also review the prerequisites for managed and custom models.

kb = agent.create_knowledge_base(
    name="anycompany-assistant-docs",
    description="AnyCompany internal documents: HR policies, IT guides, engineering runbooks, sales plans.",
    roleArn=kb_service_role_arn,
    knowledgeBaseConfiguration={
        "type": "MANAGED",
        "managedKnowledgeBaseConfiguration": {"embeddingModelType": "MANAGED"},
    },
)["knowledgeBase"]

Documents live in the bucket under docs/<folder>/. Amazon S3 has no permission system of its own to crawl, so you supply the ACLs in a global ACL file in the same bucket. Each entry maps an S3 prefix to the emails that may read it:

[
  {"keyPrefix": "s3://BUCKET/docs/hr/",
   "aclEntries": [{"Name": "maya@example.com",  "Type": "USER", "Access": "ALLOW"},
                  {"Name": "liam@example.com",  "Type": "USER", "Access": "ALLOW"},
                  {"Name": "sofia@example.com", "Type": "USER", "Access": "ALLOW"}]},
  {"keyPrefix": "s3://BUCKET/docs/engineering/",
   "aclEntries": [{"Name": "maya@example.com",  "Type": "USER", "Access": "ALLOW"},
                  {"Name": "liam@example.com",  "Type": "USER", "Access": "ALLOW"}]},
  {"keyPrefix": "s3://BUCKET/docs/sales/",
   "aclEntries": [{"Name": "sofia@example.com", "Type": "USER", "Access": "ALLOW"}]}
]

The sample’s file also gives everyone docs/it/. Then create the data source. For a managed knowledge base, every connector has the type MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR, and connectorParameters.type picks the source:

ds = agent.create_data_source(
    knowledgeBaseId=kb["knowledgeBaseId"],
    name="s3-docs-acl",
    dataSourceConfiguration={
        "type": "MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR",
        "managedKnowledgeBaseConnectorConfiguration": {
            "connectorParameters": {
                "type": "S3",
                "version": "1",
                "connectionConfiguration": {"bucketName": BUCKET, "bucketOwnerAccountId": ACCOUNT_ID},
                "filterConfiguration": {"inclusionPrefixes": ["docs/"]},
                "aclEnabled": True,
                "aclConfiguration": {"globalAccessControlListS3Uri": f"s3://{BUCKET}/acl/global-acl.json"},
            }
        },
    },
)["dataSource"]

aclEnabled cannot be changed after the data source is created. CreateDataSource is asynchronous, so wait for the status AVAILABLE. Then call StartIngestionJob and wait for COMPLETE. The sync reads the documents and the ACL file and indexes each document with its ACL. In the sample, all 11 documents were scanned and indexed with 0 failures. A document that no ACL entry covers is not ingested, and a user whose email matches no entry receives no results from this data source.

The same model applies to connectors that crawl permissions from the source system, such as Microsoft SharePoint, Google Drive, and Atlassian Confluence. There, the permissions come from the source, groups are resolved from the source, and the knowledge base also checks each result against the source in real time. Your application code does not change: it still passes the user’s email in userContext. For the full list, see Access Control Lists awareness enablement.

Step 2: Create the memory resource and design namespaces

One memory resource serves every user. Per-user separation comes from {actorId} in the namespace templates, which AgentCore memory resolves from each event at extraction time. Two choices matter.

Strategies. The two strategies extract different things. The summary strategy summarizes each conversation, so it captures facts that a user mentions in passing, such as “I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.” Those facts are what personalize a later answer about, say, PTO. The user-preference strategy extracts stated preferences into structured records (“Prefers short bullet-point answers without tables”, “Always deploys to eu-central-1 first”) and does not treat incidental mentions as preferences. Summaries give you “what we discussed.” Preferences give you “how this person wants to be answered.” Use both.

Layout. retrievalConfigs accepts one entry, so a single namespacePath must reach everything the planner should see for a user. Put {actorId} directly under the root: namespacePath: "/anycompany/<sub>" then covers the profile and every conversation summary. A layout such as /anycompany/profile/{actorId} and /anycompany/summaries/{actorId} would let one entry reach only one of them.

memory = control.create_memory(
    name="anycompany_assistant_memory",
    eventExpiryDuration=30,          # days; raw conversation events expire after this
    # encryptionKeyArn=CMK_ARN,      # optional customer managed key
    memoryStrategies=[
        {"userPreferenceMemoryStrategy": {
            "name": "EmployeeProfile",
            "namespaces": ["/anycompany/{actorId}/profile"],
        }},
        {"summaryMemoryStrategy": {
            "name": "ConversationSummaries",
            "namespaces": ["/anycompany/{actorId}/summaries/{sessionId}"],
        }},
    ],
)["memory"]

Wait for the memory to reach ACTIVE. Creating the memory does not need a user or actorId, so the order of Step 2 and Step 3 does not matter. Nothing is provisioned per user: a new Cognito user becomes a new actor the first time they ask a question.

Step 3: Set up Cognito and grant the application permissions

Create a user pool and an app client without a client secret. The email decides which documents a user may read, so make it required, verified, and not changeable by the user:

pool_id = idp.create_user_pool(
    PoolName="anycompany-assistant-employees",
    AutoVerifiedAttributes=["email"],
    Schema=[{"Name": "email", "Required": True, "Mutable": False, "AttributeDataType": "String"}],
    AdminCreateUserConfig={"AllowAdminCreateUserOnly": True},
)["UserPool"]["Id"]

Mutable cannot be changed after the pool is created. With a mutable email, a signed-in user could change their email to a colleague’s address. If your users federate from Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, map the IdP’s email to this attribute so that it matches the email in your data source’s ACLs.

The sample enables USER_PASSWORD_AUTH so the local UI and tests can sign in directly. Production applications typically use Cognito managed login or AWS Amplify.

Set up an IAM role for the application. The backend assumes it once per user, with the session tag userId=<sub>, and every memory statement is conditioned on that tag. This is the complete policy the sample runs with:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "AgenticRetrieve", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "bedrock:AgenticRetrieveStream", "Resource": "*" },
    { "Sid": "KnowledgeBaseRetrieval", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["bedrock:Retrieve", "bedrock:GetDocumentContent"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock:us-west-2:111122223333:knowledge-base/KB_ID" },
    { "Sid": "PlannerAndGeneration", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream", "Resource": "*" },
    { "Sid": "MemoryDescribe", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:GetMemory",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:111122223333:memory/MEMORY_ID" },
    { "Sid": "MemorySessionsScopedToCaller", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["bedrock-agentcore:ListEvents", "bedrock-agentcore:CreateEvent",
                 "bedrock-agentcore:ListSessions"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:111122223333:memory/MEMORY_ID",
      "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"bedrock-agentcore:actorId": "${aws:PrincipalTag/userId}"}} },
    { "Sid": "MemoryRecordsScopedToCaller", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["bedrock-agentcore:RetrieveMemoryRecords", "bedrock-agentcore:ListMemoryRecords"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:111122223333:memory/MEMORY_ID",
      "Condition": {"StringLike": {"bedrock-agentcore:namespacePath": "/anycompany/${aws:PrincipalTag/userId}/*"}} }
  ]
}

ListEvents is required with sessionBinding, RetrieveMemoryRecords with retrievalConfigs, and CreateEvent when persistenceMode is DEFAULT. ListSessions and ListMemoryRecords are for the application’s own reads (conversation list and the “what memory knows about you” view), not for AgenticRetrieveStream. The role’s trust policy allows sts:AssumeRole, sts:TagSession, and sts:SetSourceIdentity from the backend’s own identity (an AWS Lambda execution role or an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task role in production). If the memory uses a customer managed key, add kms:Decrypt on that key.

Step 4: Read the user from the token, then build the request

Verify the ID token and read the two claims. Only the ID token carries email. The access token does not:

@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class Principal:
    sub: str     # -> memory actorId and namespace
    email: str   # -> userContext.userId (document ACLs)

    def namespace_path(self, root: str) -> str:
        return f"{root}/{self.sub}"       # resolved literal, e.g. /anycompany/a8e1b390-...


def verify(id_token: str) -> Principal:
    key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(id_token)   # public keys from {issuer}/.well-known/jwks.json
    claims = jwt.decode(id_token, key.key, algorithms=["RS256"], issuer=ISSUER, audience=CLIENT_ID)
    if claims.get("token_use") != "id" or claims.get("email_verified") is not True:
        raise PermissionError("a verified ID token is required")
    return Principal(sub=claims["sub"], email=claims["email"].lower())

jwt.decode checks the signature, the issuer (your user pool), the expiry, and the audience (your app client). For details of the claims, see Understanding the identity (ID) token. With API Gateway, a JWT authorizer does the same checks and passes the claims to your handler.

Next, get the user’s AWS credentials. The backend assumes the application role for this user and caches the session until shortly before it expires:

creds = sts.assume_role(
    RoleArn=APP_ROLE_ARN,
    RoleSessionName=f"user-{principal.sub}",
    SourceIdentity=principal.sub,
    Tags=[{"Key": "userId", "Value": principal.sub}],
)["Credentials"]

Every call for this user, including the memory calls that agentic retrieval makes on the caller’s behalf, now runs as assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user-<sub> and carries the tag that the policy in Step 3 checks.

Decide the sessionId. For a new conversation, the application generates one, such as "conv-" + uuid4().hex, and returns it to the client. To continue a conversation, the client sends it back. To show a user their conversations, call ListSessions with the user’s actorId:

def list_conversations(principal):
    try:
        resp = memory.list_sessions(memoryId=MEMORY_ID, actorId=principal.sub, maxResults=50)
    except memory.exceptions.ResourceNotFoundException:
        return []   # the user has not asked anything yet, so there is no actor
    return [{"sessionId": s["sessionId"], "createdAt": s["createdAt"].isoformat()} for s in resp["sessionSummaries"]]

You do not need your own table that maps users to sessions. Accepting a sessionId from the client is safe because short-term memory is keyed by (memoryId, actorId, sessionId), and the actorId comes from the token. If Liam sends Maya’s sessionId, it names a session inside Liam’s own space, which is empty. Agentic retrieval itself does not verify that the actorId, sessionId, or namespace you supply belong to the user who is asking, so they must never come from the client. Keep your own session table only if you need data that memory does not hold, such as conversation titles.

Then build the request:

def build_request(principal, question, session_id):
    return {
        # With sessionBinding, messages carries ONLY the current question.
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": {"text": question}}],
        "retrievers": [{"configuration": {"knowledgeBase": {"knowledgeBaseId": KB_ID}},
                        "description": KB_DESCRIPTION}],
        # Document ACLs: only documents this email may read are retrieved.
        "userContext": {"userId": principal.email},
        "agenticRetrieveConfiguration": {
            "foundationModelType": "MANAGED",
            "rerankingModelType": "MANAGED",
            "maxAgentIteration": 3,
        },
        "generateResponse": True,
        "memoryConfiguration": {
            "memoryId": MEMORY_ID,
            "sessionBinding": {"actorId": principal.sub, "sessionId": session_id},
            "persistenceMode": "DEFAULT",
            "retrievalConfigs": [{"namespacePath": principal.namespace_path("/anycompany")}],
        },
    }

Without userContext, an ACL-enabled data source returns no results at all. Compare the request with the stateless handler it replaces:

history = history_table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("sessionId").eq(session_id))
messages = [*replay(history), {"role": "user", "content": {"text": question}}]
response = runtime.agentic_retrieve_stream(messages=messages, retrievers=..., agenticRetrieveConfiguration=...)
history_table.put_item(Item={"sessionId": session_id, "q": question, "a": consume(response)})

The query before the call and the write after it are gone, and messages has one element. Three rules come with sessionBinding, and each is enforced with a specific ValidationException. First, messages carries only the current question, so you choose one history source per request. Second, persistenceMode: DEFAULT (the default) writes the question and the generated answer as one event, so it requires generateResponse: true. Third, memoryId alone is invalid. persistenceMode: NONE restores history and writes nothing, for audit or replay views.

Step 5: Update the client contract and render history

The client sends { question, sessionId? }. On a new conversation, the application generates a sessionId and returns it as the first streamed frame. The client echoes it on later turns and omits it to start over.

Because the memory resource is yours, the application reads it directly to render a conversation:

def conversation_history(principal, session_id):
    resp = memory.list_events(memoryId=MEMORY_ID, actorId=principal.sub, sessionId=session_id,
                              includePayloads=True, maxResults=100)
    return [{"role": p["conversational"]["role"].lower(), "text": p["conversational"]["content"]["text"]}
            for ev in sorted(resp["events"], key=lambda e: e["eventTimestamp"])
            for p in ev["payload"] if "conversational" in p]

Each persisted turn is exactly one event with two payloads: the user’s question and the final answer. The history therefore renders as a clean transcript and remains usable by other AgentCore memory clients.

Step 6: Verify from the trace

The trace tells you, per turn, what the knowledge base and memory did:

Trace eventWhen it appearsWhat to look at
SessionHistoryLoadFirst event, whenever sessionBinding is set_memory_event_count and _memory_message_count, both 0 on a new session
SpeculativeRetrievalBefore planningOn a new session, retrievalMetadata also lists BedrockAgentCoreMemory. Memory items carry _memory_* metadata and no text. Knowledge base items carry _source_uri
PlanningEach iterationactions[].memoryRetrieve means the planner chose to search memory, with a query it composed
Retrieval with retrievalType: BedrockAgentCoreMemoryPer planned memory action_memory_record_count. A count of 0 is a normal result
A memory event with status: FAILEDMemory unavailable or access deniedfailures[].message. Memory is best-effort: the request continues and the answer is generated from the knowledge base

The following runs show the behavior. Excerpts are verbatim, trimmed for length.

Document ACLs: Maya and Sofia, same question. “What is the weekly on-call stipend?” The on-call guide is in docs/engineering/. Maya’s retrieval included docs/engineering/oncall.md, and the answer was “500 USD or 450 EUR per week.” Sofia’s speculative retrieval and the planner’s follow-up sub-query returned only HR and sales chunks:

Planning/SUCCEEDED   actions: retrieve("on-call stipend compensation policy")
Retrieval/SUCCEEDED  [BedrockKnowledgeBase]  9 items   # docs/hr/*, docs/sales/commission-plan.md

Her answer said that no on-call stipend is documented in the sources she can access. The application made no access decision. It passed userContext.userId: "sofia@example.com", and the knowledge base did the filtering. The reverse holds for the commission plan: Sofia gets the 12% accelerator, and Maya’s retrieval does not contain docs/sales/.

Turn 1: Maya, new conversation. “How do I set up the VPN on my laptop? I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.”

SessionHistoryLoad/SUCCEEDED    "Restored 0 short-term memory event(s)"
SpeculativeRetrieval/SUCCEEDED  [BedrockAgentCoreMemory, BedrockKnowledgeBase]  10 items
Planning/SUCCEEDED

The answer gives the Frankfurt gateway (vpn-fra.anycompany.example) and the macOS steps. Afterwards, ListEvents on the session shows one event with two payloads.

Turn 2: Maya, same conversation. “It keeps disconnecting every few minutes. What should I try?” The request carried only that sentence:

{"step": "SessionHistoryLoad", "status": "SUCCEEDED",
 "message": "Restored 1 short-term memory event(s)",
 "retrievalResponse": [{"metadata": {"_memory_session_id": "conv-d25dccca6cbf47a6af893621e546905d",
                                     "_memory_event_count": 1, "_memory_message_count": 2}}]}

The planner sent retrieve("VPN disconnects every few minutes troubleshooting") and retrieve("Cisco Secure Client macOS frequent disconnect fix"). The answer resolved “it” and pointed at iCloud Private Relay, the macOS-specific cause in the guide. On a continued session, SpeculativeRetrieval queries only the knowledge base. The long-term memory lookup in that step happens on new sessions.

Turn 3: Maya, a new conversation, later. “How many days of PTO do I get per year, and do unused days carry over?” Her office decides the answer, and she never mentioned it in this conversation. Speculative retrieval searched long-term memory with the raw question and found one record:

{"step": "SpeculativeRetrieval",
 "retrievalMetadata": [{"identifier": "JQUFTMTNZV", "retrievalType": "BedrockKnowledgeBase"},
                       {"identifier": "anycompany_assistant_memory-5llXYu8f2i", "retrievalType": "BedrockAgentCoreMemory"}],
 "retrievalResponse": [
   {"content": {"mimeType": "text/plain", "text": "# AnyCompany Paid Time Off (PTO) Policy ..."},
    "metadata": {"_document_title": "pto-policy.md", "_data_source_type": "S3",
                 "_source_uri": "https://.../docs/hr/pto-policy.md"},
    "sourceRetriever": {"identifier": "JQUFTMTNZV"}},
   {"content": {"mimeType": "text/plain"},
    "metadata": {"_memory_strategy_id": "ConversationSummaries-JFDHQVB4VU",
                 "_memory_query": "How many days of PTO do I get per year, and do unused days carry over?",
                 "_memory_namespace_path": "/anycompany/a8e1b390-10f1-70d9-ee85-b68b610ee0c4",
                 "_memory_record_count": 1},
    "sourceRetriever": {"identifier": "anycompany_assistant_memory-5llXYu8f2i"}}]}

Knowledge base and memory items share one retrievalResponse. Tell them apart by sourceRetriever.identifier or by the _memory_* keys. The record was the summary of her VPN conversation. That was enough: the planner went straight to the answer, which said “Since your memory indicates you’re based in the Frankfurt office … you get 30 days of PTO per year, granted in full on January 1, and any unused days must be used by March 31 of the following year.” A fact from an IT conversation personalized an HR answer.

Turn 4: Liam, new conversation, identical question. Same handler, same memory resource, a different token. Speculative retrieval found nothing about him, so the planner decided to search memory with its own query:

{"step": "Planning", "status": "SUCCEEDED",
 "actions": [{"memoryRetrieve": {"inputQuery": {"text": "employee office location"},
                                 "memoryId": "anycompany_assistant_memory-5llXYu8f2i"}}]}
{"step": "Retrieval", "status": "SUCCEEDED",
 "message": "Retrieved 0 long-term memory record(s)",
 "retrievalMetadata": [{"identifier": "anycompany_assistant_memory-5llXYu8f2i", "retrievalType": "BedrockAgentCoreMemory"}],
 "retrievalResponse": []}

Liam received the table of all three offices and a request to say which one he is in. The application chooses where the planner may look. The planner decides whether to look and what to ask: a memoryRetrieve action appears only when the planner decides that another memory search would help. Reading Maya’s sessionId through the history endpoint with Liam’s token returned an empty list.

Figure 3: The same question from two users. Maya’s trace shows a memory hit and a Frankfurt-specific answer. Liam’s trace shows zero memory records and the generic table.

Long-term extraction is asynchronous and runs after the turn is persisted. In our run, the first record appeared 81 seconds after turn 2, but the timing is not a commitment. Design for eventual availability. A fact stated in this conversation is not guaranteed to be retrievable in the next one immediately. The sample polls ListMemoryRecords before running turn 3.

Security and multi-user isolation

In this walkthrough, the application authenticates. The knowledge base filters. ACL-aware retrieval is filtering, not authorization. Take the email only from a verified ID token with email_verified: true, make it immutable in the pool, and handle email reuse: if an address is reassigned to a different person, that person gets the old owner’s document access. The knowledge base fails closed: a document with no ACL, or an ACL error, means fewer results, not extra ones. If results are missing, check that the email matches the ACL entry.

Identity comes from the token (Step 4) for memory too: actorId and namespace come from the verified sub, never from the client.

IAM condition keys, as defense in depth. AgentCore memory exposes bedrock-agentcore:actorId on ListEvents, CreateEvent, and ListSessions, and bedrock-agentcore:namespacePath on RetrieveMemoryRecords and ListMemoryRecords. The memory calls that agentic retrieval makes during a request are authorized against the calling identity. That is why the caller’s policy must grant those actions, and why the conditions in Step 3 apply to them. With the session assumed for Maya, a request bound to Maya’s actorId proceeds normally. A request that binds Liam’s actorId is the bug that this policy guards against, and it is denied at every memory operation:

SessionHistoryLoad/FAILED      failures: ["AccessDeniedException"]
SpeculativeRetrieval/SUCCEEDED failures: ["AccessDeniedException"]   # memory leg denied, KB leg answered

Nothing was written to Liam’s memory: his session count stayed at 0. The answer was still generated from the knowledge base. Because each user has their own role session, AWS also sees which user each call is for: the caller is assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user-<sub> with SourceIdentity=<sub>, which the session holder cannot change.

Two further points. The memory is a customer-owned resource that other systems in your account may also write to. Treat its contents as input, and attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the request through policyConfiguration. And plan the data lifecycle. Raw events expire per eventExpiryDuration, but extracted records do not. A user-deletion workflow therefore covers DeleteEvent for the actor’s sessions and DeleteMemoryRecord under the actor’s namespace.

Observability and failure behavior

Log the full trace with a correlation ID per turn. The planner’s sub-queries are as worth auditing as its final results. AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases reports Invocations, ClientErrors, and TotalIterationCount for Operation=AgenticRetrieveStream. AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore reports Invocations, Latency, Errors, and UserErrors per memory operation, and InputTokenUsage/OutputTokenUsage per strategy for extraction. With Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, shows a turn’s spans end to end.

Memory operations are best-effort by design. If a memory call fails or is denied, the request does not fail. The trace carries a FAILED memory event with the failure message, and the turn continues without that memory. The answer is generated from the knowledge base. Decide whether your UI surfaces that degraded state.

Considerations

  • Use a stable sessionId for the life of a conversation. The API accepts a fresh ID per request, but a fresh ID silently breaks continuity and produces one summary record per turn.
  • Use namespacePath to reach all of a user’s long-term records. retrievalConfigs accepts one entry with up to five metadataFilters. namespace matches by prefix and namespacePath matches by hierarchy, so namespacePath fits per-user IDs under the root. Supply namespaces fully resolved, because a template such as /anycompany/{actorId} is rejected.
  • Expect only USER and ASSISTANT conversational events to be restored. Events with the TOOL or OTHER role that other systems write are skipped.
  • Keep sending messages instead of sessionBinding when your application needs to control exactly which history each request carries. For example, your existing history store may be the system of record for conversations, or you may edit or redact history before sending it. With sessionBinding, the service restores and persists the conversation for you. You can’t combine the two in one request.
  • A request can carry up to five knowledge bases. With more than one retriever, the planner routes each sub-query based on the knowledge base description, so write it carefully.
  • Plan for latency and cost. The session restore adds on the order of 200 milliseconds. In our runs, a full turn with one knowledge base, ACLs, and memory took 4–10 seconds with the managed model. Planning iterations drive that time, not memory. These are observed figures, not service commitments. Agentic retrieval is priced per call plus underlying retrievals, and the memory operations made during the call are billed as AgentCore memory usage. For details, see Amazon Bedrock pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

Clean up

Run python infra/teardown.py in the sample to delete the knowledge base, the S3 bucket and its objects, the memory resource (including conversation history and long-term records), the Cognito user pool, and the IAM roles.

Conclusion

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base already gave you the retrieval stack as a service. That stack covers ingestion, document ACLs, indexing, ranking, and the planning loop in AgenticRetrieveStream that turns a hard question into a cited answer. With memoryConfiguration, the same call now carries the conversation and the user’s history. For a multi-user application, that removed the conversation store, the history replay, and the extraction pipeline. What remained was a short list of responsibilities. Authenticate the user and read two claims from the ID token: pass the verified email as userContext so that the knowledge base filters documents, and use the sub as the actorId for one memory resource with {actorId}-rooted namespaces. Use IAM condition keys on a per-user role session as a second line of defense that holds through the agentic path.

To get started, deploy the sample from the GitHub repository. Then read the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference, Access Control Lists awareness enablement, and Use AgentCore memory with agentic retrieval. For the retrieval loop itself, see Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. For memory concepts, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory: Building context-aware agents.

About the authors
